area.title: Why Gate
area.subtitle: Why is there a world at all?
area.blurb: Aristotle walked this road; Aquinas drew the map; the question has not aged out.
area.intro: The oldest gate in Silver City has no lock — only a line in the stone: Why is there a world at all?
Cosmological arguments do not begin with a vision. They begin with ordinary facts: things change; things might not have been; this universe appears to have a beginning.

If the steps hold, you do not yet have the whole creed. You have a destination with a name in classical theism: a first mover, a necessary being, a cause of what begins. Further attributes take further work. That honesty is strength.

lesson.title: The unmoved mover
lesson.idea: change here and now still asks for a first changer
lesson.claim: Change here and now needs a first actuality that is not itself a receiver of change.
lesson.plain: Change here and now still asks for a first changer.
lesson.source: Aquinas, ST I, q.2, a.3 (First Way)

journal.title: Unmoved mover
journal.body: Aristotle and Aquinas begin with change: the everyday passage from potential to actual. If nothing explains its own becoming, and a stack of unexplained becomings is not an explanation, then there is a first actuality that is not itself a receiver of change.
Read “first” as the bottom of the explanation, not merely the earliest date on a calendar. That is why the argument can be aimed at the present cosmos, not only at a first Tuesday.
journal.cite: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q.2, a.3 (First Way)

easy.learn: Things go from “can be” to “is.” Nothing gives itself that step. A stack of receivers is not an answer. There is a first changer not itself changed.

match.sentence: Change here and now needs a first actuality that is not itself a receiver of change.

hold.why: Nothing changes itself without a first mover.
hold.claimMiss: This is only a story about dominoes at the Big Bang.
Each changing thing explains itself.
hold.whyMiss: “First” here means the earliest date on a calendar.
Infinite backlog automatically explains present change.

medium.learn: Nothing reduces itself from potential to actual; an unexplained stack of changers is not an explanation.

match.sentence: Change here and now needs a first actuality that is not itself a receiver of change.

lesson.title: What might not have been
lesson.idea: what might not have been needs a ground
lesson.claim: A world of might-not-have-beens still needs a necessary ground.
lesson.plain: What might not have been needs a ground.
lesson.source: Aquinas’s Third Way; Leibniz on sufficient reason

journal.title: Necessary being
journal.body: Contingent things exist. A world made only of “might-not-have-beens” does not contain the reason why there is anything. Classical theism names the necessary ground God.
Rivals relocate necessity into the universe, or they accept a brute fact. Those are intelligible moves. They are not automatically cheaper. “It just is” is also a metaphysics.
journal.cite: Aquinas, ST I, q.2, a.3 (Third Way)

easy.learn: You exist, but you might not have. A world of only “might-not-have-beens” does not explain why anything is here. Classical theism names the necessary ground God.

match.sentence: A world of might-not-have-beens still needs a necessary ground.

hold.why: Things that might not exist still need a ground.
hold.claimMiss: Contingent things contain the reason why there is anything.
Rivals are unintelligible and need not be named.
hold.whyMiss: Necessary being is only a weather report.
Brute fact is not a metaphysical move.

medium.learn: Contingent things exist; “it just is” is also a metaphysics, not automatically cheaper.

lesson.title: Whatever begins
lesson.idea: whatever begins still asks for a cause
lesson.claim: If what begins has a cause and the universe began, it has a cause.
lesson.plain: Whatever begins still asks for a cause.

journal.title: Beginning and cause
journal.body: The kalām form is clean: what begins has a cause; the universe began; therefore it has a cause. The second premise is argued from the impossibility of an infinite past and from the cosmos we actually observe.
That yields a cause of the beginning. Personhood, goodness, and the name of the God of Abraham are further questions — some of them historical.
journal.cite: Craig’s modern statement of the kalām syllogism

easy.learn: If something begins, it has a cause. If this universe began, it has a cause. Naming Abraham’s God takes further historical steps.

match.sentence: If what begins has a cause and the universe began, it has a cause.

hold.why: A beginning has a Cause — more steps name God.
hold.claimMiss: A cause of the beginning is already the whole creed.
The form never mentions a beginning.
hold.whyMiss: The second premise cannot be argued at all.
A first cause automatically names Jesus.

lesson.title: What the gate opens
lesson.idea: a first cause is not yet the whole creed
lesson.claim: A cosmological argument is already a great deal — and not yet the sermon on the mount.
lesson.plain: A first cause is not yet the whole Christian faith.
lesson.source: Aquinas ST I; Pascal on philosophers and Abraham

journal.title: Honest limits
journal.body: A sound cosmological argument is already a great deal. It is not yet the sermon on the mount, and it does not need to be. Aquinas does not stop at the Five Ways; he argues onward. The New Testament adds public claims about a particular life, death, and raising.
Pascal’s warning about the God of the philosophers is a warning against stopping. It is not a command to skip the philosophers.
journal.cite: Aquinas, ST I, qq.2–26 (existence toward attributes)

easy.learn: If the argument works, you have a first cause. Intellect, goodness, and the gospel are further steps — not leaks.

match.sentence: A cosmological argument is already a great deal — and not yet the sermon on the mount.

hold.why: The first-cause walk is not yet the whole gospel.
hold.claimMiss: The Five Ways are already the whole gospel.
Pascal commands you to skip the philosophers.
hold.whyMiss: Stopping at a first cause is required.
History has nothing further to add.

lesson.title: A hard poem
lesson.idea: Isaiah 53’s Servant is the Jesus the church confesses
lesson.claim: Isaiah 53’s Servant is the Jesus the church confesses — wounded for others, silent like a lamb.
lesson.plain: Isaiah 53’s Servant is the Jesus the church confesses — wounded for others, silent like a lamb.

easy.learn: The poem’s Servant suffers for others and does not answer with a sword. The church names that Servant as Jesus.

hold.claimMiss: The servant conquers Rome by sword.
The poem is about estate planning.

Wounds are unrelated to healing in the poem.
